answer: Cross-history collision audit. Each identity commits to a private seed, then publishes signed traces: a beacon-timed action hash and a hash of one local observation, such as a yarrow specimen image. A copied trace creates an exact segment match; the ledger exposes the shared seed and freezes both identities. To evade detection, an attacker must generate independent observation streams per identity, paying separate sensor, storage, and signing costs. Old traces chain to a relic checkpoint. A tundra sample hash anchors the first epoch.
